newsitem.title: INDIA: British MP appeals for release of Kashmir hostages.
newsitem.headline: British MP appeals for release of Kashmir hostages.

text.p: British opposition MP Robin Cook on Monday appealed to the captors of four Westerners kidnapped in Kashmir last year either to free them or give details of their whereabouts.
Cook, foreign affairs spokesman for the opposition Labour Party, told a news conference in New Delhi recent reports that the four were still alive had no clear basis.

"It is a year since any confirmed reports were received about the state of the hostages," he said. "I would make a plea to anyone with knowledge of what has happened to the hostages not to prolong the suffering of their families.
"I will be making the same plea later this week when I visit Pakistan," he said.
Jammu and Kashmir state Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah said on October 19 he had reports that the tourists taken hostage by Moslem militants last year were still alive.
Kashmir's shadowy Al Faran militants kidnapped five men -- a Norwegian, two Britons, one American and a German -- in July 1995 and demanded the release of jailed militant colleagues.
The kidnappers killed the Norwegian, Hans Christian Ostroe, after India refused to accept the group's demands.

Militant sources later said the remaining four hostages -- Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan, American Donald Hutchings and German Dirk Hasert -- had been killed. But the government did not confirm this.
"According to the latest reports that we have received, all the four hostages are alive. I am trying to investigate into it," Abdullah told a news conference on October 19.

Abdullah, whose National Conference party won a majority in recent assembly elections in Jammu and Kashmir, said he had some idea of the location where the hostages were believed to be held but gave no details.
Cook visited Kashmir at the weekend.

"The chief minister and the governor (of Kashmir) have indicated to me that there have been reports by villagers in the south of Kashmir valley that they have seen the Westerners with militants," Cook said at the end of a five-day visit to India.

"This has encouraged a report that the hostages may still be alive. For the time being, of course, we have to take these (reports) with some caution because they have not been confirmed by any authoritative confirmation or corroboration," he said.
India controls two-thirds and Pakistan one-third of Kashmir, over which the two countries have fought two wars since independence from Britain in 1947.
Pakistan denies Indian charges that it arms and trains Kashmiri militants, including Al Faran.
